name: zipper
intent: Represent a position inside an immutable tree as a focused subtree paired with the reversed path to the root, so that navigating and editing nearby nodes costs one step instead of copying the path from the root for every change.
problem: Updating a nested immutable structure by path is O(depth) per edit and forces the root to be threaded through every function: a walk that touches dozens of nearby nodes rebuilds the same spine again and again, and code that wants to remember where it was (editor caret, rewrite position, undo entry) has to carry a path by hand at each call site. A fixed-path update helper also only ever addresses one hard-coded route through the tree.
context: Immutable or persistent data structures - ASTs, document and JSON/XML trees, widget and scene hierarchies, proof terms - where one logical actor navigates and edits a small region of a large structure and the location itself is the natural handle. The pattern is the functional answer to the mutable cursor: it keeps referential transparency and structural sharing but restores local, incremental editing, which is why structured editors, refactoring tools and comonadic UIs are its classic homes. It is irrelevant when the structure is mutable in place or when every edit path is known statically.
benefits: Each navigation or editing step is O(1) - move a frame, rebuild only the enclosing node - instead of O(depth) per edit for root-based path updates.
The location is a first-class value: it can be stored, returned, serialised as an edit position or pushed onto a history stack, which makes undo/redo a matter of keeping the previous location.
Referential transparency is preserved: no node is mutated, earlier locations keep denoting the version they were taken from, and unchanged subtrees stay shared.

The surrounding context becomes explicit and inspectable - parent, siblings, ancestors - so "replace this subtree", "insert a sibling here" and "move this subtree next to that sibling" are local operations rather than whole-tree rewrites.
Independent locations over the same tree can be processed in parallel without locks, because nothing is shared mutably.
It generalises to any recursive structure (lists, trees, JSON, terms) by deriving the context type from the node type's shape, so one mental model covers many editors.
tradeoffs: A second, mutually recursive type must be defined and kept in step with the node type: every node constructor needs a matching context case, so adding a variant of the data touches the zipper too.
Getting the tree back (top/root/unzip) walks the whole path: O(depth) once. Code that zips and unzips in a loop is slower than the naive root-based update it was meant to beat.
Movement is partial: up at the root or left at the first sibling is meaningless, so every move has to express failure (Option/Maybe/Result, a null, or an exception) and callers pay for edge handling.
Locations are version-bound snapshots, not stable references: a location captured before another edit points into the old tree, and keeping it alive keeps that whole version reachable.
The context exposes enclosing structure that a pure tree hides, so code that should see only a subtree can climb out of its scope - encapsulation must be re-established with navigation verbs.
Navigation frames cost memory proportional to depth, and in languages without a GC the path frames need explicit ownership handling.

participants.responsibility: The subtree (or item) currently addressed; edits apply here and only here, and the focus is never modified in place.
The reversed path from the focus to the root: one frame per level recording the parent's own data and the sibling subtrees left behind, so the ancestor can be reconstructed without the subtree.
The value pairing focus and context; it denotes exactly one position in exactly one version of the tree, and navigation and edits consume it and return a new location.
down/up/left/right (plus depth-first next/prev) that push or pop a context frame; partial at the boundaries, so they report failure in the return type or offer a separate safe/unsafe pair.
Replace or update the focus, insert or delete a child or sibling, detach and attach subtrees; each returns a new location whose context is rebuilt for the edited level.
Reconstructs a complete tree from a location by folding the context back over the focus; the only operation that walks the path, and the point at which the new version is published.

use_cases: Structured text editors whose buffer is a tree (document to paragraphs to tokens): the caret is a location and a keystroke edits one node instead of rebuilding the document.
AST rewriting and refactoring tools that walk a parse tree and patch many nodes: every patch is local and the tree is rebuilt once at the end.
Document editors for JSON/XML where a position must be stored, put on an undo stack or sent over the wire, because focus plus path is a serialisable description of where the user is.
Immediate-mode and comonadic UIs: the focused path from the root is exactly the context that rendering and event routing need for a widget tree.
Proof assistants, type checkers and compilers that walk a term while keeping the surrounding goal or typing context available.
Scene graphs and ECS-style editors keeping a "current entity" cursor over an immutable hierarchy for spawning, reparenting and reordering nodes.

Clojure's standard library ships clojure.zip so application code edits nested vectors, sequences and XML through a location value: seq-zip, vector-zip and xml-zip build it, up/down/left/right navigate it, edit, insert-child and replace patch the focus, and root() rebuilds the updated document.

GHC's Core simplifier carries SimplCont - the strict evaluation context 'above' the hole being simplified - which the simplifier threads through expressions zipper-style so inlining, eta-expansion and rule firing can consult what remains around the focus instead of re-walking the spine from the root.

The Rust list-zipper crate turns any IntoIterator source into a cursor: the focused element moves forwards and backwards in O(1) with the elements behind it held on a reversed list - the zipper specialised from trees to sequences.
avoid_when: The tree is mutable and shallow (arrays of objects, DOM-style node graphs): mutate in place; the zipper exists to avoid copying, not to add ceremony to a structure that is already edited locally.
Only one fixed path is ever updated (one nested field): a Lens or a plain copy-with helper expresses that as a constant chain of accessors, and the extra context type is pure overhead.
The structure is parsed, transformed and printed in one pass: a recursive fold over the tree is shorter and equally fast, because the result is a new tree anyway.
Every edit is applied in a single sweep from the root: an accumulating traversal avoids the second type and keeps the code in one function.
The structure is flat or one level deep: index arithmetic on a list already gives O(1) moves.
anti_patterns: Zip/unzip ping-pong: calling root() after every small edit, which pays O(depth) per change and throws away the locality the pattern was adopted for.
An "immutable" API over nodes that other code still mutates: previously captured locations change meaning silently.
Treating a location as a stable identifier - storing it in a map or comparing locations taken before and after an edit - when it is a snapshot-bound position, not an entity reference.
Adding parent pointers to a nominally immutable tree instead of an explicit context: cycles leak, structural sharing breaks and serialisation of the tree fails.
Using the zipper as the general iteration device for read-only walks, allocating context frames where a fold or an iterator would do.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: what is being looked at (the focus) is separate from where it sits (the context).
Immutability and persistence: every operation returns a new value and never mutates shared structure.
Make partiality explicit: boundary moves are represented in the return type rather than being undefined behaviour or an unnoticed null.
Representation invariant: focus plus context always denote exactly one position in exactly one tree version.
Closed data modelling: the context is the node type's one-hole context, which keeps navigation and rebuild total over a closed set of node shapes.
best_practices: Keep navigation and editing pure: consume a location and return a new one; never write into a node payload.
Batch edits while located and rebuild the tree once (top/root/unzip) - O(depth) per batch, not per edit.

Model the context from the node's own shape (one frame kind per node case), or implement a generic protocol - clojure.zip's branch?/children/make-node - so one zipper serves arrays, JSON documents and ASTs.
Provide safe moves that report failure in the return type plus one documented unsafe variant for hot paths, instead of letting a boundary move fail implicitly.
Keep the location type out of the model's public API: expose navigation verbs and hand back the root only when the caller commits.
Make deep navigations iterative with an explicit frame loop rather than relying on recursive descent, so tree depth is bounded by memory rather than by the stack.
sources: Huet, G., The Zipper, Journal of Functional Programming 7(5), pp. 549-554, 1997 (Functional Pearl) - the originating paper: the tree is turned inside out so that a location holds the focused subtree and its reversed path to the root.

McBride, C., The Derivative of a Regular Type is its Type of One-Hole Contexts (extended abstract) - http://strictlypositive.org/diff.pdf - the zipper generalised: the one-hole contexts of a regular type are its syntactic derivative.

McBride, C., Clowns to the Left of me, Jokers to the Right (Functional Pearl) - https://personal.cis.strath.ac.uk/conor.mcbride/Dissect.pdf - dissections refine the one-hole context into direction-aware left and right contexts.

Hinze, R., Jones, C. C., Loitsch, R., Generic 'Zipper': the context of a traversal - https://okmij.org/ftp/continuations/zipper.html - generalises the zipper from data to traversals and shows where Huet's data-centric construction falls short.

https://downloads.haskell.org/~ghc/9.6.6/docs/libraries/ghc-9.6.6/src/GHC.Core.Opt.Simplify.Utils.html - GHC simplifier source: SimplCont is the strict evaluation context used zipper-like around the current hole.
https://docs.rs/list-zipper/latest/list_zipper/ - list-zipper crate documentation: an O(1)-move cursor over any sequenceable source.
